title: Migration: the animals that travel across the world every year

summary.text: Every year, an Arctic tern flies from the top of the world to the bottom and back, about 70,000 kilometres. Humpback whales swim thousands of kilometres between cold seas full of food and warm seas where their calves are born. Monarch butterflies make a journey so long that it takes their great-grandchildren to finish it. These yearly journeys are called migration. Animals migrate to find food, warmth and safe places to raise their young, and many young birds find the right part of the world on their first journey, alone.
summary.art: A world map with three dotted journey lines: an Arctic tern from the far north to Antarctica, a humpback whale from a cold sea to a warm one, and a monarch butterfly from Canada to Mexico.

intro.hook: Each winter, a small grey bird called a curlew sandpiper lands on a mudflat at Kodiakkarai, at the tip of Tamil Nadu. She has flown there from the far north of Russia, more than 6,000 kilometres away. Some of these birds are only a few months old. They have never seen Kodiakkarai, and no grown-up bird showed them the way. So how did they know where to go?
intro.text: Animals of every kind make long journeys each year: birds, whales, butterflies, dragonflies, turtles, fish, and people too. In this unit you will meet the record travellers, find out why they go, and test two ways of finding your way in your own home.
intro.art: A small grey sandpiper with a long, thin, curved beak, standing on wet mud at the edge of the sea at sunrise, with a lighthouse far behind.

outcomes: I can say what migration is, and name birds, whales, butterflies and other animals, including people, that make long journeys every year.
I can explain why animals migrate, to find food, warmth and safe places for their young, and what the journey costs them.
I can describe some record journeys: the Arctic tern, the humpback whale, the monarch butterfly and the globe skimmer dragonfly. I can say which are known for sure and which are still being checked.
I can explain the difference between following a direction and knowing a place, using my own moved-start test.
I can say how scientists follow travelling animals: rings, tags, trackers and help from ordinary people.
I can explain how wind helps travellers, using my paper butterfly test.
I can name ways people help or harm travelling animals: resting lakes, bright lights and busy roads.

terms.meaning: A long journey that an animal makes at the same time each year, from one place to another and back again.
terms.example: Every winter, demoiselle cranes fly from Central Asia over the Himalayas to Rajasthan. In spring they fly back. That is migration.
terms.art: A line of grey cranes with long necks flying over snowy mountains.

terms.meaning: To make a migration. An animal that migrates is called a migrant.
terms.example: Barn swallows migrate to South India for the winter, and leave again in spring.
terms.art: Swallows with long forked tails sitting on an electric wire in a row.

terms.meaning: The way a traveller goes from one place to another.
terms.example: The route of a monarch butterfly runs from Canada, through the United States, to the mountains of Mexico.
terms.art: A dotted line on a map with small arrows, from one city to another.

terms.meaning: A wide path across the world that many kinds of migrating birds use every year.
terms.example: India lies on the Central Asian Flyway. Millions of birds come down it each winter, from Russia and Central Asia to Indian lakes and coasts.
terms.art: A broad band drawn across a map from northern Russia down to India, with many small birds along it.

terms.meaning: The place where an animal lays eggs or gives birth, and raises their young.
terms.example: The curlew sandpiper's breeding ground is the Arctic tundra in the far north of Russia.
terms.art: A small bird sitting on a nest of eggs on flat, mossy, treeless ground.

terms.meaning: The place where a migrating animal spends the cold months, often far from where they breed.
terms.example: Chilika Lake in Odisha is a wintering ground for hundreds of thousands of ducks and other water birds.
terms.art: A wide lake full of ducks and waders, with fishing boats at the far edge.

terms.meaning: A place on the route where a traveller rests and eats before going on.
terms.example: Many birds flying from Central Asia stop at lakes in Gujarat and Rajasthan, eat for a few days, and then fly further south.
terms.art: Tired birds feeding in shallow water at a small lake, halfway along a dotted route on a map.

terms.meaning: To find your way from one place to another. The finding of the way is called navigation.
terms.example: A young cuckoo navigates all the way to Africa on her first journey, alone.
terms.art: A bird flying over the sea at night with stars above and a faint arrow showing her direction.

terms.meaning: Something you can see, hear or smell that tells you where you are: a hill, a river, a building or a coast.
terms.example: On the way to school, the big banyan tree and the temple gopuram are landmarks that tell you that you are nearly there.
terms.art: A street with a big banyan tree and a tall temple tower, with a child pointing at them.

terms.meaning: The way something is pointing or moving: towards the sea, towards the sunrise, north or south.
terms.example: From Kodiakkarai, the Arctic coast of Russia lies to the north. A bird flying there must keep heading north for thousands of kilometres.
terms.art: A compass rose with four arrows marked N, S, E and W.

terms.meaning: Something an animal has from birth, without being taught. Scientists also say innate.
terms.example: A young cuckoo is raised by other birds. Yet she flies the right way to Africa, so the direction must be inborn.
terms.art: A very young bird looking up at the sky, with a faint arrow drawn inside her chest pointing south.

terms.meaning: A wind that blows from behind, the same way you are going. It pushes you along. A wind in your face is a headwind.
terms.example: Cycling with a tailwind is easy. Cycling into a headwind is hard work.
terms.art: A child cycling with a flag on the cycle streaming forward, and wind lines coming from behind.

terms.meaning: All the animals or people born at about the same time. Your parents are one generation, you are the next, and your grandparents are the one before.
terms.example: The monarch journey north takes three or four generations of butterflies.
terms.art: Four butterflies in a row, each a little further along a map, with a heart between each pair.

terms.meaning: A tiny machine fixed to an animal. The tracker records where the animal goes, and sometimes sends that record to scientists by satellite.
terms.example: Scientists fixed trackers on Amur falcons in Nagaland and followed them all the way to southern Africa.
terms.art: A small falcon in the sky with a tiny box and a thin aerial on her back.

terms.meaning: Tiny shrimp-like animals that live in huge numbers in cold seas. Many whales eat them.
terms.example: A blue whale can eat several tonnes of krill in a day in the cold seas near Antarctica.
terms.art: A swarm of tiny pink shrimp-like animals in dark blue water, with a whale's open mouth nearby.

explanations.definition: Migration is a long journey that an animal makes at about the same time every year, from one place to another, and back again.
explanations.description: A crow flying across the city to find food is not migrating. She comes home the same evening. A migration is a big, regular journey that follows the seasons. Most migrants live in two homes: one where they raise their young, and one where they spend the rest of the year. Some go north and south. Some go up mountains in summer and down in winter. Some fish swim from the sea up a river.
examples: Demoiselle cranes spend the summer in Central Asia and Mongolia, where they raise their chicks. They spend the winter in India, and thousands of them come to the village of Khichan in Rajasthan.
Hilsa fish live in the Bay of Bengal. In the monsoon, many swim up rivers such as the Hooghly to lay their eggs.
A house crow stays in the same city all year. She is not a migrant.
explanations.art: Two homes on a map joined by a curved arrow going one way and another arrow coming back, a nest at one end and a lake at the other.
explanations.context: This card says what migration means, and what does not count as migration.

explanations.definition: Animals migrate to be where food, warmth and safe places for their young are, at the time of year when they need them.
explanations.description: In the far north, summer brings long days, plenty of insects and space to nest. Then winter comes. The ground freezes and the food is gone. So many birds raise their chicks in the north in summer and fly south for the winter, where there is still food. Whales do something similar in the sea. The cold seas near the poles are full of food in summer, while warm seas are safer places for a newborn calf. Many scientists think the main reason is food, not cold. A bird with enough food can survive a lot of cold.
examples: Curlew sandpipers nest in the Arctic, where the summer brings swarms of insects for their chicks. In winter they come to Indian coasts, where the mud is full of worms and tiny shellfish.
Humpback whales eat krill in cold seas, then swim to warm seas where their calves are born.
explanations.art: A see-saw with a nest and summer insects on one side, and a warm mudflat full of worms on the other, with a bird flying between them.
explanations.context: This card says why animals make such long and difficult journeys.

explanations.definition: Migration costs a lot of energy and is dangerous. Many travellers die on the way. It is still worth it for those who make it, because of what waits at the other end.
explanations.description: Before a long flight, a bird eats and eats, and stores the food as fat under her skin. The fat is fuel for the journey. On the way there are storms, hunters, tall glass buildings, bright city lights and lakes that have dried up. A young bird on her first journey is in the most danger. So why go? Because staying would be worse. A bird who stays where the food runs out may starve. Every journey is a choice between two risks.
examples: In 2022, a young bar-tailed godwit flew from Alaska to Tasmania without stopping, more than 13,000 kilometres in 11 days. She could not eat, drink or rest on the way.
A humpback whale mother may eat almost nothing for months while she is in the warm sea with her calf, living on her fat.
explanations.art: A small bird with a round belly of stored fat, and beside her a fuel gauge reading full.
explanations.context: This card is about how hard migration is, and why animals do it anyway.

explanations.definition: Some animals make journeys of thousands of kilometres every year. Scientists know this because they have followed them with rings, tags and trackers.
explanations.description: The Arctic tern makes the longest yearly journey known. In 2010, scientists fixed tiny trackers to terns in Greenland. The birds flew to Antarctica and back, about 70,000 kilometres in a year. A tern can live 30 years, so in a lifetime she may fly as far as the Moon and back three times. Humpback whales swim up to about 8,000 kilometres each way between cold seas and warm seas. Monarch butterflies fly up to about 4,000 kilometres from Canada and the United States to the mountains of Mexico.
examples: An Arctic tern sees two summers every year: the Arctic summer and the Antarctic summer.
Bar-headed geese fly over the Himalayas, some of the highest mountains on Earth, to spend the winter in India.
explanations.art: A globe with a long looping line for an Arctic tern, a shorter one in the sea for a whale, and one over America for a monarch.
explanations.context: This card meets the animals that make the longest journeys.

explanations.concept: A journey longer than one life
explanations.definition: For some insects, one journey takes several generations. The children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren carry it on.
explanations.description: In autumn, monarch butterflies fly south to the mountains of Mexico. These autumn monarchs live about 8 months, much longer than summer monarchs, who live only a few weeks. In spring they fly north, lay eggs on the way, and die. Their children fly further north and lay eggs. It takes three or four generations to reach Canada. Then, in autumn, the great-great-grandchildren fly all the way back to the same mountains in Mexico, a place none of them has ever seen.
examples: A monarch who reaches Canada in summer is the great-granddaughter of the monarch who left Mexico in spring.
Painted lady butterflies also travel over many generations, between Africa and Europe.
explanations.art: Four butterflies along a map from Mexico to Canada, each a different colour, joined by small eggs between them.
explanations.context: This card is about journeys that are too long for one life.

explanations.concept: Two ways to find the way: a direction, or a place
explanations.definition: A traveller can find the way by keeping a direction for a certain distance, or by knowing the place itself. Young birds on their first journey use mostly the first. Older birds also know places.
explanations.description: Picture walking to a bowl by counting 6 steps from a doorstep. That works only if you start from the doorstep. If someone moves you without telling you, the same 6 steps take you to the wrong spot. But if you can see the bowl, you can walk to it from anywhere. Young birds on their first journey carry a direction and a distance inside them from birth. Older birds have learned the places too, so they can correct a wrong start.
examples: In the 1950s, the Dutch scientist A.C. Perdeck caught thousands of starlings in the Netherlands in autumn and flew them to Switzerland. The young ones kept their usual direction and ended up in Spain and the south of France. The adults turned towards their real winter home in the north of France and England.
A young common cuckoo is raised by other birds and never meets her parents. She still flies to Africa alone, in the right direction.
explanations.art: Two dotted arrows on a map: one young bird following a straight arrow from a wrong start and missing a lake, and an older bird bending towards the lake.
explanations.context: This card explains the two ways of finding the way that you tested with the bowl.

explanations.concept: What tells a bird which way to go?
explanations.description: Scientists agree that migrating birds use several clues: where the Sun is, the patterns of the stars at night, the Earth's magnetism, smells and landmarks such as coasts and mountains. They still argue about how birds sense the Earth's magnetism, and about which clue matters most.
examples: Birds kept in a cage at migration time hop towards the side of the cage that points the way they would fly.
A compass needle lines up with the Earth's magnetism. Many birds seem able to sense the same magnetism.

perspectives.who: Many scientists who study the eyes of birds
perspectives.explanation: A protein in a bird's eyes, called cryptochrome, changes with the Earth's magnetism. So the bird may see the magnetism as a faint pattern over what she sees.
Some birds may sense magnetism with nerves in their beak, or in their ears. More than one sense may be at work.
Some sea birds seem to find their way by smells carried on the wind. When they cannot smell, they get lost more often.

explanations.art: A bird flying at night with the stars above, faint curved magnetic lines around the Earth below, and a coastline far ahead.
explanations.context: This card is about how birds know which way to fly. Scientists know some answers and still argue about others.

explanations.definition: A wind blowing the way a traveller is going, a tailwind, carries them along and saves energy. Many migrants wait for the right wind before they set off.
explanations.description: A small bird or insect flies only a little faster than a strong wind. So the wind makes a big difference. With a tailwind, a bird covers more ground with the same fuel. With a headwind, she may go nowhere. Bird scientists watching radar see many more birds take off on nights when the wind blows their way. Large birds such as storks and eagles also ride on rising warm air, called thermals, so they can glide for hours without flapping.
examples: Globe skimmer dragonflies arrive in the Maldives each year with the winds from India, in October and November.
In your paper butterfly test, the same butterfly travelled further from the same height when the fan blew behind it.
explanations.art: A dragonfly flying over the sea with long wind arrows behind her, and a small island ahead.
explanations.context: This card is about how wind helps travellers, which you tested with a paper butterfly.

explanations.definition: Humans are animals, and many people make yearly journeys with the seasons, for the same reasons other animals do: food, water and work.
explanations.description: Some families of shepherds walk their flocks to new grass every year. In the summer the high mountain meadows have grass, and in winter the plains do. Many workers travel to cities for part of the year and go home for harvest or festivals. Long ago, before farming, all humans moved with the seasons, following food.
examples: Gaddi shepherds in Himachal Pradesh take their sheep and goats up to high meadows in summer and down to the warmer valleys in winter.
Dhangar shepherds in Maharashtra move their flocks across the Deccan in the dry months, looking for grass and water.
Some Kuruba shepherds in Karnataka walk their sheep to new grazing land each year.
explanations.art: A family of shepherds walking up a mountain path with a flock of sheep and goats, snowy peaks behind.
explanations.context: This card shows that humans are migrating animals too.

explanations.concept: How we know where they go
explanations.definition: Scientists follow migrating animals with numbered rings on legs, paper tags on wings, tiny trackers that talk to satellites, radar, and the help of many ordinary people.
explanations.description: A ring is a tiny metal or plastic band with a number. If the same bird is caught or found again somewhere else, the number tells where she was before. Trackers are smaller than ever, but they must be very light, or they will slow the animal down. Ordinary people help a lot. Bird watchers all over India count birds and share their lists online, so scientists can see when the travellers arrive and leave.
examples: In 2013, scientists fixed trackers on Amur falcons in Nagaland and followed them across the Arabian Sea to southern Africa.
Volunteers in America and Canada stuck tiny paper tags on monarch butterflies, which led to the discovery of their winter forests in Mexico.
explanations.art: A bird scientist's hands gently holding a small bird, with a tiny numbered ring on one leg.
explanations.context: This card says how people find out where migrating animals go.

agreed.text: Many kinds of birds, whales, fish, insects, turtles and mammals, including humans, make long journeys at about the same time each year.
agreed.evidence: Rings, tags and trackers have followed these animals for over a hundred years, and bird watchers count their arrival every season.

agreed.text: Animals migrate mostly to be where there is food and a safe place to raise their young at that time of year.
agreed.evidence: Migrants arrive where food is plentiful and leave as it runs out. Where food stays all year, many of the same kinds stay put.

agreed.text: Many young birds on their first journey fly in an inborn direction, without being shown the way.
agreed.evidence: Young cuckoos raised by other birds fly to Africa alone. Young starlings moved to Switzerland kept their usual direction and missed their usual winter home.

agreed.text: Migrating birds use several clues to find their way, including the Sun, the stars, the Earth's magnetism and landmarks.
agreed.evidence: In experiments, birds change the direction they try to fly when scientists change the star pattern above them in a planetarium, or change the magnetism around them.

agreed.text: Lost resting places, bright lights at night, glass buildings and hunting kill many migrating animals.
agreed.evidence: Scientists count birds killed at lit buildings, and see numbers fall where wetlands on the route have dried up or been built over.

challenging.claim: A butterfly is too light and fragile to fly thousands of kilometres.
challenging.who: Many people, before the monarch's winter forests were found in 1975
challenging.for: A butterfly weighs about half a gram, and summer butterflies live only a few weeks.
challenging.against: Tagged monarchs have been found thousands of kilometres from where they were tagged. The autumn monarchs live about 8 months, long enough for the journey.
challenging.context: This card looks at an old idea about whether small insects can travel far.

challenging.claim: Every young bird learns the route by following their parents.
challenging.for: Young cranes and geese do fly with their families, and learn the stopovers on the way.
challenging.against: Young cuckoos never meet their parents, and young curlew sandpipers fly south weeks after the adults have left. They still reach the right part of the world.
challenging.context: This card asks whether young birds always learn the way from grown-ups.

challenging.claim: Migrating animals always go north in summer and south in winter.
challenging.for: Many birds that come to India do fly south in autumn and north in spring.
challenging.against: Some birds move up mountains in summer and down in winter. Blue tiger butterflies in South India move between the plains and the Western Ghats. Arctic terns go to the far south for the southern summer.
challenging.context: This card looks at which directions migrants really go.

challenging.claim: Globe skimmer dragonflies cross the ocean from India to East Africa and back every year.
challenging.who: Charles Anderson, a marine biologist in the Maldives, in 2009
challenging.for: Huge numbers of globe skimmers appear in the Maldives each October, with the winds from India, though the islands have almost no fresh water for them to breed in. Later studies of the dragonflies' wings supported a long journey.
challenging.against: No one has followed a single dragonfly the whole way. The round trip would take about four generations, and parts of it are still guesses.
challenging.context: This card is about a journey that may be the longest made by any insect, and that scientists are still checking.

challenging.claim: Birds sense the Earth's magnetism with a protein in their eyes.
challenging.who: Many scientists who study bird senses
challenging.for: A protein called cryptochrome in birds' eyes changes with magnetism. Some birds lose their magnetic sense in some colours of light.
challenging.against: No one has yet shown exactly how the bird turns this into a sense of direction. Other senses in the beak or the ear may help too.
challenging.context: This card is about how birds might sense the Earth's magnetism.

big_questions.q: A young cuckoo flies to Africa alone, the right way, without ever meeting her parents. Where is the map: inside her, or out in the world?
big_questions.hint: Think about your test. Your counted steps were inside you. The bowl was out in the room. Which one did you need when you were moved?

big_questions.q: When you were moved to a new start, your steps went wrong. Did your steps make a mistake, or did the world around them change?
big_questions.hint: Your steps were the same as before. What was different?

big_questions.q: The monarch who leaves Mexico in spring never reaches Canada. Her great-granddaughter does. Whose journey is it?
big_questions.hint: Is a journey something one traveller does, or something a whole family carries on?

big_questions.q: An Arctic tern follows the summer around the world and sees two summers every year. What would your year be like if you followed the summer?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you would miss, and what you would gain.

big_questions.q: Shepherds, fishers and workers in India travel with the seasons too. Can a journey you make every year be a kind of home?
big_questions.hint: Ask someone in your family who goes to the same place every year what it feels like when they arrive.

big_questions.q: Bright city lights at night can confuse birds that fly by the stars. Who should the night sky belong to?
big_questions.hint: Think about people who work at night, birds that fly at night, and the stars themselves.

story.title: The Ring at Kodiakkarai
story.note: Curlew sandpipers really do breed in the Arctic tundra of Russia and spend the winter on Indian coasts, including Point Calimere (Kodiakkarai), where bird scientists have ringed waders for many years. In this kind of bird, the adults leave the Arctic first and the young fly south weeks later, on their own. Lost young birds far from their usual range are found more often than lost adults. The starling experiment Chitti mentions was done by A.C. Perdeck in the Netherlands and published in 1958. Harini, Arun and Chitti Selvi are made up.
text: Every winter, Harini's aunt went to work at Kodiakkarai. Kodiakkarai is at the very tip of Tamil Nadu, where the land points out into the sea. Its other name is Point Calimere. Harini called her aunt Chitti, which means mother's younger sister in Tamil. This year, for the first time, Harini and her little brother Arun went with her.

Chitti Selvi was a bird scientist. In the cool months, the mudflats at Kodiakkarai fill with small grey birds. They run along the edge of the water, poking the wet mud with long, thin, curved beaks. 'These are curlew sandpipers,' Chitti said. 'Each one weighs about as much as a small tomato.'

Before sunrise, Chitti and two other scientists, Mary and Nandini, had put up a long, soft net across the mudflat. It was so fine that it was hard to see. A few sandpipers flew into it and were caught, gently, like a ball in a cloth. The scientists lifted them out one by one with careful fingers. Harini held her breath.

Chitti weighed each bird in a little cloth bag and measured her wing. Then she slipped a tiny metal band onto one leg and squeezed it shut with special pliers. 'This is a ring,' she said. 'It has a number on it, like a car's number plate. If anyone catches this bird again, anywhere in the world, the number tells them where she has been.'

Then Nandini held up a bird and laughed. 'This one already has a ring!' Chitti read out the number, and Mary looked it up in a thick notebook. There was a long silence. Then Mary said, 'We ringed her right here. On this same mudflat. Two winters ago.'

Harini looked at the small grey bird. 'So she has been here before?' 'Yes,' said Chitti. 'Since then she has flown to the far north of Russia twice, to the Arctic, more than six thousand kilometres away. She laid her eggs there on the open ground, in the short Arctic summer. Then she flew all the way back. Not just to India. To this mudflat.'

'How did she find it?' asked Harini. 'There are thousands of beaches.' Chitti let the bird go, and she flew off low over the water. 'She knows this place,' said Chitti. 'The shape of the coast, the lighthouse, perhaps the smell of the mud. Older birds remember places.'

Arun was frowning. 'But what about the baby birds? The ones who have never been here?' Chitti smiled. 'That is the strange part. In this kind of bird, the parents leave the Arctic first. The young ones stay behind and eat and grow. A few weeks later, they fly south on their own. Nobody shows them the way.'

'Then how do they know where to go?' asked Arun. 'Scientists think the young are born knowing which direction to fly, and for about how long,' said Chitti. 'It is like a rule inside them: fly this way, for this many nights. Most of them reach the right part of the world by following that rule.'

Harini thought about this all through lunch, which was fish curry and rice at a small hotel by the jetty. Then she asked, 'Chitti, what if a storm blows a young bird a long way sideways?' 'Then she may keep flying her direction from the wrong place,' said Chitti. 'She would land somewhere new, far from her kind. Bird watchers sometimes find a lost young bird like that. Older birds are much better at finding their way back, because they know the places.'

That evening, on the verandah of the forest guest house, Harini had an idea. She put a steel tumbler at the far end of the verandah. 'Arun, this is the mudflat. You are a young sandpiper. Stand on the doorstep.' Arun stood on the doorstep, and Harini taught him to walk straight to the tumbler. It took him 6 steps.
Then she tied her dupatta over his eyes. 'Don't peek. Walk your 6 steps.' Arun walked 6 steps and stopped. The tumbler was right by his toes. 'Easy,' he said.

'Again,' said Harini. This time she led him around in a little circle, still with his eyes covered. Then, very quietly, she stood him two big steps to the left of the doorstep, facing the same way as before. 'Walk your 6 steps.' Arun walked 6 steps and stopped. Harini laughed. The tumbler was far away to his right.
Arun pulled off the dupatta. 'That's not fair! You moved me!' 'That is what the storm did to the young bird,' said Harini. 'Your steps were right. Your start was wrong.'

'Do it once more,' said Arun. Harini moved him again, to a new spot. This time, before she covered his eyes, she let him look for three seconds. He turned a little, and walked straight to the tumbler.

Arun stood still for a moment. 'So I knew two different things,' he said slowly. 'I knew the steps. And when I peeked, I knew the place.' 'That is it exactly,' said Chitti, who had been watching from the doorway. 'More than sixty years ago, a Dutch scientist found the same thing with starlings. The young ones knew a direction. The old ones also knew the place.'

The next morning, a big flock of sandpipers lifted off the mudflat all at once, turned in the light, and settled again further along. Somewhere among them was the bird with the old ring. Harini wondered where the young ones would go in spring, and whether, two winters from now, one of them would come back to this very mud, knowing the place.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Arun's counted steps worked only from the usual start, like a young bird's inborn direction. Moved without knowing, he missed. One look at the tumbler let him find it from anywhere, like an older bird who knows the place. Knowing a way and knowing a place are two different kinds of knowing.
ask: How did the scientists know the ringed sandpiper had been at Kodiakkarai before?
Why did Arun miss the tumbler the second time, even though he walked his 6 steps?
What helped Arun find the tumbler the third time?
Which part of Arun's game was like a young bird, and which was like an older bird?
If you were a young sandpiper, would you rather fly with the old birds or alone? Why?

games.title: The Butterfly Relay: Mexico to Canada and back
games.context: This is a board game about the monarch butterfly's journey. The trip north is a relay: each butterfly flies part of the way, lays eggs, and hands over to the next generation. Then one autumn generation flies the whole way back.

printables.title: A board with 20 squares, from Mexico to Canada and back
items: Square 0: The fir forests in the mountains of Mexico, the start. Every player's butterfly begins here in spring.
Square 1: Warm sunshine. Fly on.
Square 2: Milkweed plants in Texas. Your butterfly lays eggs here. Hand over to the next player: this is the end of the first generation's leg.
Square 3: A thunderstorm. Miss a turn: the turn passes to the next player, with no question.
Square 4: A field of flowers. Drink nectar. Roll again.
Square 5: A busy highway. Go back 1.
Square 6: A tailwind from the south. Move on 2.
Square 7: Milkweed plants in Oklahoma. Lay eggs. Hand over: end of the second generation's leg.
Square 8: A garden where the gardener sprayed poison. Go back 2.
Square 9: A school garden full of milkweed. Roll again.
Square 10: Cold night. Miss a turn while the butterfly warms up in the sun.
Square 11: Milkweed near the Great Lakes. Lay eggs. Hand over: end of the third generation's leg.
Square 12: A volunteer sticks a tiny tag on your wing. Take a tag token.

items: The butterfly who spent the winter in Mexico
Her children
Her grandchildren
Her great-grandchildren
The autumn generation: her great-great-grandchildren
Tag token 1

rules: You need the board, the question cards, one dice and the butterfly tokens. Put the butterfly who spent the winter in Mexico on square 0. There is only one butterfly on the board at a time.
Players take turns in order. On your turn, another player reads you the top question card. Playing alone? Read it yourself and check the back. When the cards run out, shuffle them and use them again.
Answer right, and roll the dice and move the butterfly. Answer wrong, and read the back aloud. The butterfly stays.
Do what the square says. If that sends you to another square, do not do that square as well.

On a 'Lay eggs' square, the butterfly stops there even if the roll was bigger. Swap in the next generation: her children, then her grandchildren, then her great-grandchildren. The turn then passes to the next player as usual.
At square 15, swap in the autumn generation. This one butterfly flies all the way back to Mexico.
If you land on square 12, take a tag token. At the end, every tag token is a butterfly that scientists could follow. There are only 4 tags: when they are gone, nothing happens on square 12.
Everyone wins together when the autumn butterfly reaches square 19. You do not need the exact roll: reaching or passing 19 ends the game.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the board. 2. Put the butterfly who spent the winter in Mexico on square 0. 3. Shuffle the cards and put them face down.
flow.say: In spring, monarch butterflies leave their winter forests in Mexico. No single butterfly will reach Canada. Let's see why.
flow.kid: Put the winter butterfly on square 0. Mix up the cards. You are a monarch!
flow.context: This is the first step of The Butterfly Relay, a board game about the monarch's journey over many generations.

flow.do: Play a practice card: 'How many generations does the monarch journey north take?'
flow.say: Practice card. How many generations does the trip north take?
flow.kid: Practice card. How many generations fly north? Say your answer.

check.q: How many generations of monarchs does it take to fly from Mexico to Canada?
check.why: Each spring and summer monarch lives only a few weeks. She flies part of the way, lays eggs, and dies. Her children carry on. It takes three or four generations to reach Canada.

flow.do: Play the game until the autumn butterfly reaches square 19. Pause at each 'Lay eggs' square.
flow.say: You've reached milkweed. Your butterfly lays eggs here. Who carries the journey on now?
flow.kid: Lay eggs! Swap in the next butterfly. Then the next player takes a turn.

ask.q: The butterfly who left Mexico never reaches Canada. Who does?
good: Her great-granddaughter.
The third or fourth generation.

flow.do: When the game ends, talk about the autumn generation.
flow.say: The autumn butterfly flew all the way back to forests she had never seen. How do you think she knew where to go?
flow.kid: Your autumn butterfly never saw Mexico. How did she find the way?

ask.q: How could an autumn monarch find a forest she has never seen?
good: She was born knowing the direction.
She follows the Sun and keeps flying the right way.

flow.parent: Scientists have found that monarchs use the Sun to keep their direction, together with a clock in their bodies. How they find the very same forests is still not fully known.

flow.kid: Take a card. Read it. Stay or go? Say why.

flow.kid: Why did you choose that? What if she stayed?

flow.do: Look at which cards were STAY. What do they have in common?
flow.say: Look at all the STAY cards. What do they have that the GO cards don't?
flow.kid: Look at the STAY cards. What do they all have?

ask.q: What do the animals that stay have in common?

Their home doesn't get too cold or too dry.

experiments.title: Moved in the Night: do your steps still find the bowl from a new start?
experiments.context: In this experiment you learn to walk to a bowl by counting steps. Then a grown-up secretly moves your starting spot, the way a storm can blow a young bird off course. You measure how far from the bowl you end up.
experiments.question: If you learn to reach a bowl by counting your steps, can you still find the bowl when someone moves your starting spot without telling you?
experiments.predict: Guess first. When your eyes are covered and you start from a new spot, will your usual steps still take you to the bowl? If not, how far away will you stop? And if you peek at the bowl for three seconds first, what will happen? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every walk uses the same number of steps, the same cloth over your eyes, and your normal walking speed. Only one thing changes: where you start, and whether you peek. Try each way 3 times, because one try can be a fluke.
results_table: How far from the bowl you stopped (in foot-lengths)

materials.item: a steel bowl, plate or tumbler: this is the 'lake'
a dupatta, scarf or soft cloth to cover the eyes
two sheets of newspaper or two strips of tape, to mark two starting spots
a clear stretch of floor about 3 to 4 metres long: a hall, a corridor or a room with the chairs pushed back
a pencil and the results table in a notebook

experiments.safety: The walker cannot see. Clear the floor of toys, slippers and wires first. A grown-up walks beside the child every time, ready to stop them before a wall or a table.

schedule.what: Learn the steps to the bowl. Walk them 3 times from the usual start, 3 times from a secret new start, and 3 times from a new start after a peek. Measure each time.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw the floor from above: the bowl, the two starts, and a dot where you stopped each time.

flow.do: 1. Clear the floor. 2. Put the bowl at one end. 3. Put a newspaper sheet about 5 or 6 normal steps away, facing the bowl. This is the usual start. Keep the second sheet for later.
flow.say: Here is our lake, and here is where a young bird starts her journey. Let's set it up carefully first.
flow.kid: Put the bowl at the end of the room. This is the lake. Stand on the newspaper. That is your start.
flow.parent: Use your child's own foot for measuring. One metre is about 4 or 5 of a child's foot-lengths. If your room is small, put the bowl 4 steps away and move the secret start 3 foot-lengths.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Moved in the Night experiment. You set up a 'lake' and two starting spots.

flow.do: 1. Stand your child on the usual start, facing the bowl. 2. Let them walk to the bowl with eyes open, three times. 3. Count the steps together. Write the number down.
flow.say: Walk to the lake with your eyes open. Count your steps out loud. Do it three times, so the number stays in your head.
flow.kid: Walk to the bowl. Count your steps out loud. Do it three times. How many steps is it?

ask.q: How many steps does it take you to reach the bowl?
good: The same number each time, about 5 or 6.
It was 6 the first time and 6 again.

flow.parent: Ask them to take normal steps, not giant ones, so the count stays the same.

flow.do: Before any test, ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess at the top of the table.
flow.say: Soon I will cover your eyes and maybe move you. Do you think your steps will still find the lake? Why?
flow.kid: Your eyes will be covered. You might be moved. Will your steps still find the bowl? Why do you think so?

ask.q: What do you think will happen if I move you without telling you?
good: I will miss the bowl, because my steps go the same way.
I will still find it, because I remember where it is.

flow.parent: Don't say which guess is right. The test will answer it.

flow.do: 1. Cover your child's eyes with the cloth. 2. Turn them slowly round twice and walk them about the room for a few seconds, as in the next step. Then stand them on the usual start, facing the bowl. 3. Say 'Walk your steps.' 4. When they stop, measure how far their toes are from the bowl in your foot-lengths. 5. Do it 3 times and write each number.
flow.say: Eyes covered. You are on the usual start. Walk your steps, then stop. I'll measure how close you are.
flow.kid: Eyes covered. Walk your steps. Stop. How close are you to the bowl?
flow.parent: Walk beside them with a hand ready. Most children stop within 1 or 2 foot-lengths of the bowl. A step drifting a little to one side is normal.

flow.do: 1. Cover your child's eyes. 2. Turn them slowly round twice and walk them about the room for a few seconds. 3. While they are turning, put the second sheet about one metre to one side of the usual start, facing the same way. 4. Quietly stand them on this secret start. 5. Say 'Walk your steps.' 6. Measure and write. 7. Do this 3 times. Each time, walk them about first.
flow.say: I'm going to walk you about a little. Then you start again. Walk your steps, and stop.
flow.kid: Keep your eyes covered. I will walk you about. Then walk your steps and stop.

check.q: From the secret start, you walked your usual steps. Where did you stop?
options: Right next to the bowl, as before
About as far to one side of the bowl as the start had been moved
Nowhere near, in a random place
check.why: Your steps took you the same direction and distance as before. But they began one metre to the side, so they ended about one metre to the side. If you picked 'right next to the bowl', that was a good guess, but your steps don't know where the bowl is. They only know which way and how far.

flow.parent: Make sure the secret start faces exactly the same way as the usual start. Children usually stop 3 to 5 foot-lengths to one side of the bowl. That is the result to look for.

flow.do: 1. Cover your child's eyes, turn them round twice and walk them about, as before. 2. Stand them on the secret start, facing the same way as the usual start. 3. Uncover their eyes for three seconds to look at the bowl. 4. Cover their eyes again and say 'Now find the bowl.' 5. Measure and write. 6. Do this 3 times.
flow.say: This time you get a quick peek at the lake first, only three seconds. Then find it with your eyes covered.
flow.kid: Look at the bowl for three seconds. Now eyes covered. Find the bowl!

ask.q: What did you do differently after the peek?
good: I turned a little towards the bowl before walking.
I walked to where I saw it, not just my steps.

flow.do: Look at the three rows of numbers together. Ask your child to say what they found as a claim, the evidence and the reason.
flow.say: Look at our numbers. Say what you found, which numbers show it, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Look at your numbers. What did you find? Which numbers show it? Why?

ask.q: Why did your steps miss the bowl from the secret start, but not after the peek?
good: The steps only know which way and how far, so a new start sends them to a new place.
When I peeked, I knew where the bowl was, so I could find it from anywhere.

flow.think: A young bird on her first journey flies a direction she was born with. What would happen to her if a storm moved her?
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the steps carried a direction and a distance, and that the peek gave the place. This is the difference between a young bird and an older one.

experiments.title: Wind at Your Back: how much further does a tailwind carry a paper butterfly?
experiments.context: In this experiment you drop a paper butterfly from the same height, first with no wind, then with a fan blowing from behind. You measure how far from the spot below your hand she lands.
experiments.question: How much further does a falling paper butterfly travel when a wind blows from behind?
experiments.predict: Guess first. With no wind, where will the butterfly land? With the fan blowing behind it, how far will it go: a little further, twice as far, or more? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same butterfly, dropped from the same height, from the same spot, every time. Keep the fan at the same speed and the same distance. Only the wind changes. Drop it 3 times each way, because one drop can be a fluke.
results_table: How far from the spot below the hand it landed (cm)

materials.item: a square of thin paper, about 10 cm by 10 cm: tissue paper, a paper napkin or thin printer paper
a paper clip or a hair clip, to pinch the paper in the middle
a table fan or pedestal fan, or a hair dryer on its cool setting
a measuring tape or a 30 cm ruler
a coin or bottle cap to mark the spot under the hand

experiments.safety: A grown-up sets up and switches on the fan. Keep fingers and paper away from the blades.

schedule.what: Make a paper butterfly. Drop it 3 times with no wind and 3 times with a fan blowing behind it. Measure each landing.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the two kinds of drop side by side, with an arrow for the wind.

flow.do: 1. Pinch the paper square in the middle to make two wings. 2. Clip the middle with a paper clip. 3. Switch off the ceiling fan and close the windows.
flow.say: Let's make a butterfly. The clip is her body. We switch off the ceiling fan, so only our own wind blows.
flow.kid: Pinch the paper in the middle. Clip it. Now you have a butterfly!
flow.context: This is the first step of the Wind at Your Back experiment. You make a paper butterfly to drop.

flow.do: 1. Stand in one spot. 2. Hold the butterfly at shoulder height with your arm straight out. 3. Put a coin on the floor right under your hand.
flow.say: Hold the butterfly with your arm straight out. The coin marks the spot right under it.
flow.kid: Hold out your arm. Put a coin under your hand. That is the start spot.
flow.parent: Keep the same height every time. Shoulder height with a straight arm is easy to repeat.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason, and write it down.
flow.say: Where will the butterfly land with no wind? And with the fan behind her? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Where will she land with no wind? And with wind behind? Why?

flow.do: 1. Drop the butterfly with no fan on. 2. Measure from the coin to where it landed, in centimetres. 3. Do it 3 times. Write each number.
flow.say: Let go, don't throw. Then measure how far it landed from the coin.
flow.kid: Let go gently. Don't throw! Measure from the coin. Do it 3 times.
flow.parent: With no wind, the butterfly usually lands within about 20 or 30 cm of the coin, wobbling on the way down.

flow.do: 1. Put the fan about one metre behind the dropper, pointing the way the butterfly will go. 2. Switch it on at its lowest speed. 3. Drop the butterfly from the same height. 4. Measure from the coin. 5. Do it 3 times.
flow.say: Now the fan is our tailwind. Same height, same spot. Let go, and measure again.
flow.kid: Now the fan blows behind you. Let go from the same spot. Measure. Do it 3 times.

check.q: With the fan blowing behind, the butterfly landed much further from the coin. Why?
options: The fan made the butterfly lighter
The moving air pushed her along while she fell
check.why: The butterfly took the same time to fall. All that time the moving air pushed her forward. A longer push means a longer journey. 'Lighter' is a common guess, but the butterfly weighs the same with or without wind.

flow.parent: On the lowest fan speed, the butterfly often lands one to two metres away. If she flies off the table or the fan is too strong, move the fan further back.

flow.do: Look at the numbers together. Work out how many times further the wind carried her. Ask for claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: How many times further did she go with the wind? What does that tell us about tiny travellers like dragonflies?
flow.kid: How much further did she go with the wind? What does that mean for a dragonfly?

ask.q: Why do many migrating birds and insects wait for a tailwind before they set off?
good: The wind carries them further for the same work.
They save fuel, so they can go further before they need to eat.

flow.think: A globe skimmer dragonfly weighs less than a paper clip. How could she cross the sea?

activities.title: Go or Stay? Sort the travellers
activities.context: A quick sorting activity to start the unit. You guess which animals make a long journey every year, and which stay in one place.

materials.item: 12 small slips of paper with an animal written on each (the list is in step 1)
two bowls or two sheets of paper labelled GO and STAY

schedule.what: Sort 12 animals into 'makes a long journey every year' and 'stays'. Then check.

activities.record: Put a tick on each slip you sorted right.

flow.do: Write one name on each of 12 slips. Bar-headed goose. Rock pigeon. Wildebeest in Africa. Indian cobra. Barn swallow. Common myna. Blue whale. House gecko. Amur falcon. Indian palm squirrel. Dhangar shepherd family. Red-vented bulbul.
flow.say: Here are 12 living beings. Some make a long journey every year. Some stay near home all year. Let's guess which.
flow.kid: Here are 12 slips. Each has a living being on it. Read them out loud.
flow.context: This is the first step of Go or Stay, a sorting activity about which animals travel far every year.

flow.do: Let your child sort the slips into GO and STAY. Ask for a reason for each one.
flow.say: Put each one in GO if you think they travel far every year, or STAY if they stay near home. Tell me why.
flow.kid: Put each slip in GO or STAY. Say why for each one.

ask.q: Why did you put the blue whale in GO?
good: Whales swim very far in the sea.
I have heard whales travel between cold and warm seas.

flow.do: Read out the answers. GO is the bar-headed goose, barn swallow, wildebeest, blue whale, Amur falcon and Dhangar shepherd family. STAY is the Indian cobra, rock pigeon, common myna, house gecko, Indian palm squirrel and red-vented bulbul.
flow.say: Let's check. Were there any surprises? A shepherd family is in GO. Humans are animals too, and some of us migrate.
flow.kid: Let's check. Were you surprised by any? People can migrate too!

check.q: Which of these makes a long journey every year?
check.why: Barn swallows spend the summer far to the north and the winter in South India. Mynas and geckos stay near the same home all year.

flow.parent: Some kinds of animals are mixed, with some travelling and some staying. If your child asks about one, say that scientists are still finding out.

activities.title: Ask an Elder: who in our family moved with the seasons?
activities.context: Humans are animals, and many people make yearly journeys. In this activity you ask an older person in your family about journeys they made every year.

materials.item: a notebook and pencil
a grandparent, parent or older neighbour to talk to, in person or on the phone

schedule.what: Ask an elder five questions about yearly journeys. Write down the answers.

activities.record: Write the answers, and draw a map with an arrow from one place to the other.

flow.do: Help your child write five questions: 1. Did you travel somewhere every year? 2. Where to? 3. What time of year? 4. Why did you go? 5. How did you find the way?
flow.say: Many people travel to the same place every year, like birds. Let's find out who in our family did.
flow.kid: Write five questions for your elder. Where did they go? When? Why? How did they know the way?
flow.context: This is the first step of Ask an Elder. You find out about yearly journeys in your own family.

flow.do: Help your child ask the questions and write short answers.
flow.say: Ask your questions slowly, and write a few words for each answer.
flow.kid: Ask each question. Listen. Write a few words for each answer.
flow.parent: Answers may be a summer trip to the native village, going home for Pongal or Durga Puja, work on a farm at harvest, or moving with cattle or sheep. All of these are yearly journeys.

flow.do: Compare the answers with a bird's migration.
flow.say: Was the reason like a bird's reason: food, work, family, or a safe home for the children?
flow.kid: Was their reason like a bird's reason? How was it the same? How was it different?

ask.q: How is your elder's yearly journey like a bird's migration?
good: They went at the same time every year, like the birds.
They went where there was work or food, like birds go where there is food.

activities.title: Landmarks on My Way: draw a route you know by heart
activities.context: Older migrating birds know landmarks: coasts, rivers and mountains. In this activity you draw the landmarks on a route you know well, and test how well you know them.

materials.item: a sheet of paper and colour pencils

schedule.what: Draw the landmarks on a route you know. Then test yourself on the next trip.

activities.record: Keep the drawing. Tick each landmark you spotted on your next trip.

flow.do: Help your child pick a route they know well (home to school, to a grandparent's house, or to the market). Ask them to draw it as a line with every landmark they remember.
flow.say: Pick a road you travel a lot. Draw it as a line. Put on every landmark you remember: a tree, a temple, a shop, a bridge.
flow.kid: Draw a road you know well. Draw everything you remember on it. A tree? A shop? A bridge?
flow.context: This is the first step of Landmarks on My Way. You draw a route you know from memory.

flow.do: Count the landmarks together. Ask which ones are seen, heard or smelled.
flow.say: Which landmarks would you know with your eyes shut? A bakery smell? Temple bells? A noisy junction?
flow.kid: Which landmarks could you find with your eyes shut? A smell? A sound?

ask.q: Which landmark would tell you that you are nearly there?
good: The big tree at the corner.
The smell of the bakery near our gate.

flow.do: On your next trip on that route, take the drawing. Tick each landmark as you pass it, and add any you forgot.
flow.say: On our next trip, let's tick each landmark. Did you forget any?
flow.kid: On your next trip, tick each landmark. Add any you forgot.
flow.wait: Do this on the next trip along the route.
flow.parent: Scientists who fixed trackers on homing pigeons near Oxford, in England, found that pigeons who knew an area kept to their own favourite routes, following landmarks they had learned.

activities.title: Winter Visitors Watch (from October to March)
activities.context: From about October to March, birds from the north visit Indian towns and cities. This is a window or balcony watch to look for them. It works best in those months.

materials.item: a window or balcony with a view of a tree, a wire or a patch of sky
a notebook and pencil
a bird book or a free bird app, if you have one

schedule.what: Watch from a window for 10 minutes. Write down every bird. Check which ones are winter visitors.

activities.record: Write each bird you saw, how many, and whether they are a winter visitor.

flow.do: Sit at a window in the early morning or late afternoon. Write down every bird you see in 10 minutes.
flow.say: Let's be bird watchers for 10 minutes. Write every bird you see, even crows and pigeons.
flow.kid: Watch from the window for 10 minutes. Write every bird you see.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Winter Visitors Watch. You count birds from a window.

flow.do: Check your list for winter visitors that often come to Indian towns (barn swallow, grey wagtail, white wagtail, brown shrike, greenish warbler, Blyth's reed warbler and rosy starling).
flow.say: Did any of our birds fly here from far away? Let's check the list of winter visitors.
flow.kid: Check your list. Did a winter visitor come to your window?
flow.parent: If you see no winter visitors, that is a real result too. Many visitors keep to lakes, fields and parks. Try once a week through the winter months.

projects.context: In this 3-day project you make a small book about one migrating animal: where they go, when, why, and the dangers on the way.

materials.item: 4 sheets of paper folded in half and stapled into a book
colour pencils
a world map: an atlas, a printed map or a map on a phone

schedule.what: Choose your traveller. Find where they breed and where they spend the rest of the year. Draw the map page.
Write and draw the journey: when they leave, what they eat, where they stop, and the dangers.
Write how scientists found out, and one thing nobody knows yet. Read your book to someone.

projects.record: The finished book, with a map, at least four pages, and one question nobody can answer yet.

flow.do: Help your child choose one traveller from this unit (Arctic tern, curlew sandpiper, demoiselle crane, humpback whale, monarch butterfly, globe skimmer dragonfly or olive ridley turtle). Draw a map page with the two homes and the route.
flow.say: Choose one traveller. Where is their summer home? Where do they go for the rest of the year? Let's draw both on a map.
flow.kid: Choose your traveller. Draw a map. Mark both homes. Draw the route between them.
flow.context: This is the first day of My Migration Book, a 3-day project about one migrating animal.

flow.do: On day 2, write and draw two pages: the journey, and its dangers.
flow.say: Today, write about the journey. When do they leave? What fuels them? What dangers are on the way?
flow.kid: Write about the journey. When do they go? What dangers are there? Draw them.

flow.do: On day 3, write how scientists found out, and one open question. Then your child reads the book aloud to someone.
flow.say: Last page: how do we know, and what is still a mystery? Then read your book to someone.
flow.kid: Write how we know. Write one mystery. Read your book to someone.

ask.q: What is one thing nobody knows yet about your traveller?
good: How a young one knows the way on the first trip.
Exactly how they sense the Earth's magnetism.

challenges.title: The Lightest Tracker: how much can a flyer carry?
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. Scientists must make trackers light enough not to slow a bird down. You test how much weight a paper plane can carry and still fly well.
challenges.problem: A tracker that is too heavy can tire a bird or make her fall behind. Find out how much extra weight a paper plane can carry before it flies much shorter, and where to put the weight so it flies best.
constraints: Use one paper plane for every test.
The 'tracker' is paper clips, taped on.
Throw from the same spot, with the same gentle push, 3 times for each test.
materials: a measuring tape, or count your steps
general: Scientists use a rule of thumb: a tracker should weigh no more than about 3 parts in every 100 of the bird's weight.
Trackers are fixed near the middle of the back, close to where the body balances, so they don't pull the bird off balance.
Solar panels on trackers mean smaller batteries, so the tracker can be lighter.
creative: Fix the clips on the middle of the plane instead of the nose or tail, and see if it balances better.
Make a lighter 'tracker' from a small scrap of foil instead of a clip, and see if the plane flies further.
Some scientists don't put trackers on birds at all. They use radar, cameras or the songs birds make at night.
challenges.your_turn: Now design the best place and the lightest tracker for your plane. Draw it, test it 3 times, and write how far it flew compared with no tracker.

flow.do: 1. Fold a simple paper plane. 2. Throw it 3 times from the same spot. 3. Measure each flight and write it down.
flow.say: First, our plane flies with no tracker. How far does it go?
flow.kid: Fold a paper plane. Throw it 3 times. How far did it go?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Lightest Tracker challenge. You test how far a paper plane flies with no extra weight.

flow.do: Tape 1 clip on the middle of the plane, then 2, then 4. Throw 3 times each, and measure.
flow.say: Now add a tracker of one clip, then two, then four. Does the plane still fly as far?
flow.kid: Tape on 1 clip. Throw 3 times. Then 2 clips. Then 4.

ask.q: How many clips made the plane fly much shorter?
good: With 4 clips it fell quickly.
It still flew well with 1 clip, but not with 4.

flow.do: Move the same 2 clips to the nose, then to the tail. Throw 3 times each.
flow.say: Does it matter where the tracker goes? Let's try the nose and the tail.
flow.kid: Move the clips to the front. Throw. Now to the back. Throw.

check.q: Why do scientists fix a tracker near the middle of a bird's back?
options: So other birds can see the tracker
check.why: Weight near the middle, where the body balances, does not tip the bird forwards or backwards. Your plane probably flew straighter with the clips near the middle too.

flow.do: Talk about your best design. Draw it.
flow.say: What was your best design? What would you tell a bird scientist?
flow.kid: Draw your best tracker. Where did you put it? Why?

challenges.title: A Safe Crossing: help travelling crabs cross the road
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. On Christmas Island, in the Indian Ocean, millions of red crabs walk from the forest to the sea each year to lay their eggs. Roads cross their way. You design a safe crossing.
challenges.problem: Every year on Christmas Island, millions of red crabs migrate from the forest to the sea, and many used to be crushed on the roads. Design a way for crabs to cross the road safely, while cars can still use it.
constraints: Build a model with cardboard, a box or books for the road.
Toy cars or small boxes must be able to drive along the road.
Paper crabs, or dried beans as crabs, must be able to get from one side to the other without going on the road.
materials: a long piece of cardboard as the road
a handful of dried beans or paper crabs
a toy car or a small box
general: A tunnel under the road, with low walls that guide the crabs to it.
A bridge over the road for crabs to climb.
Closing the road for the weeks when the crabs are walking.
creative: On Christmas Island, people built a crab bridge over a road and low fences that lead the crabs to it.
Signs and lights that warn drivers on migration nights.
A crab map, made with help from local people, of where the crabs cross most.
challenges.your_turn: Now build your own crossing. Test it: can the beans or paper crabs get across without touching the road while a toy car drives along?

flow.do: Show the problem. Lay the cardboard road between two 'forest' and 'sea' sides. Drive the toy car along while moving beans across.
flow.say: Here is the forest, here is the sea, and here is the road between. What happens to crabs who cross?
flow.kid: This is the road. The crabs must cross it. What could happen?
flow.context: This is the first step of A Safe Crossing, a design challenge for travelling animals.

flow.do: Draw three ideas before building.
flow.say: Let's draw three ideas first. Over, under, or something else?
flow.kid: Draw three ideas. Over the road? Under it? Something new?

flow.do: Build the best idea. Test it with beans and a toy car.
flow.say: Build your crossing. Then test it. Do the crabs get across while the car drives?
flow.kid: Build it. Test it with the beans and the car. Does it work?

ask.q: How do you get the crabs to use your crossing, and not walk on the road?
good: Build low walls that lead them to it.
Put the tunnel where they already cross.

flow.do: Talk about what worked and what you would change.
flow.say: What worked? What would you change? Who else might use your crossing?
flow.kid: What worked? What would you change?

check.q: Why does a crab crossing need low walls beside it?
options: To keep cars off the crossing
To lead the crabs to the crossing, so they don't walk onto the road
check.why: Crabs will not find a tunnel or bridge by chance. Low walls guide them to it. The same idea is used in many places for frogs, toads and other travelling animals.
