quiz.p: What makes a journey a migration?
opts: It is very long
It happens at about the same time every year, there and back
It is made by a bird
quiz.why: A migration is regular and seasonal, there and back. Whales, butterflies, fish and people migrate too, not only birds. 'Very long' is common, but a short yearly trip up a mountain and down again is migration too.

opts: A house crow in Chennai
A garden lizard in Madurai
A barn swallow who spends the winter in South India
quiz.why: Barn swallows come to South India for the winter and fly north in spring. Crows and garden lizards stay near the same home all year.

quiz.p: Why do humpback whales swim to warm seas?
opts: To find more krill
Their calves are born there
To escape sharks in cold seas
quiz.why: The cold seas have the krill. The warm seas are where calves are born. A mother may eat almost nothing for months while she is there, living on her fat.

quiz.p: What does a bird do before a long migration?
opts: Eats a lot and stores fat as fuel
Grows extra wings
Sleeps for a week
quiz.why: The stored fat is fuel for the journey. A bar-tailed godwit flying from Alaska to Tasmania without stopping lives on fat the whole way.

quiz.p: Which animal makes the longest yearly journey known?
opts: The Arctic tern
The house sparrow
The elephant
quiz.why: Trackers showed Arctic terns flying about 70,000 kilometres a year, from the Arctic to Antarctica and back.

quiz.p: A monarch leaves Mexico in spring. Who reaches Canada?
opts: The same butterfly
Her great-granddaughter
Nobody: monarchs never reach Canada
quiz.why: Spring and summer monarchs live only a few weeks. Each lays eggs on the way, and the journey north takes three or four generations.

quiz.p: Why do scientists say the globe skimmer's ocean crossing is 'still being checked'?
opts: Nobody has followed a single dragonfly the whole way
Dragonflies cannot fly over water
Nobody has ever seen a globe skimmer
quiz.why: There is strong evidence for the crossing, but no one has yet tracked one dragonfly all the way from India to Africa. So it is very likely, but not proved.

quiz.p: In the bowl test, you were secretly moved to a new start and walked your usual steps. What happened?
opts: I stopped right at the bowl
I stopped about as far to the side as I had been moved
I couldn't walk at all
quiz.why: Your steps carried a direction and a distance, not the place of the bowl. Start somewhere else, and they end somewhere else.

quiz.p: Young starlings moved from the Netherlands to Switzerland ended up in Spain. Adults reached their usual winter home. Why?
opts: The young were faster
The young kept their inborn direction, while the adults knew the place
The adults followed the young
quiz.why: Like your counted steps, the young birds' direction worked only from the usual start. The adults knew where their winter home was, like your peek at the bowl.

quiz.p: How could scientists find out where monarch butterflies go in winter?
opts: Volunteers tagged butterflies, and the tags pointed the way to Mexico
They followed them in an aeroplane
They read it in an old book
quiz.why: Thousands of volunteers stuck paper tags on monarchs. In 1975, Catalina Aguado and Ken Brugger found the forests in Mexico. Local people had known about them all along.

quiz.p: Why must a tracker on a bird be very light?
opts: So it doesn't slow her down or tire her
So it is cheaper
So other birds can't see it
quiz.why: A heavy tracker makes the journey harder. A rule of thumb is no more than about 3 parts in every 100 of the bird's weight.

quiz.p: Your paper butterfly landed much further with the fan behind her. Why do many migrants wait for a tailwind?
opts: It carries them further for the same effort
It makes them lighter
It keeps them warm
quiz.why: The moving air pushes them along while they fly, like the fan pushed your butterfly while she fell. Radar shows many more birds take off when the wind blows their way.

quiz.p: Which of these harms birds that migrate at night?
opts: Dark skies
Bright lights left on in tall buildings
A lake kept as a resting place
quiz.why: Bright lights confuse birds that fly by the stars, and many crash into lit buildings. Dark skies and resting lakes help them.

quiz.p: A lake where birds rest and eat on their route is called a what?
opts: A stopover
A breeding ground
A landmark
quiz.why: A stopover is a rest and refuelling place on the way. If it is drained or built over, birds from far away lose a place they need.

items.p: Which of these is a migration?
opts: A crow flying across the city to find food, and back the same evening
A crane flying from Mongolia to Rajasthan every winter, and back every spring
A family moving to a new house once
items.why: Migration is a long journey made at the same time every year, and back again. A crow's trip across town and back each day is not migration, and nor is a single move to a new house.

items.p: A long journey that an animal makes at the same time every year, and back again, is called ____.
items.why: Migration is the word for a regular, yearly journey between two homes.

items.p: Sort these journeys. Is each one a migration, or not?
items: Olive ridley turtles coming to Odisha beaches every year to lay eggs
Migration
A cow walking to the field in the morning and home in the evening
Not migration
A Gaddi family taking sheep to the high meadows every summer
Migration
A bee flying from her hive to the flowers and back every day
Not migration
Amur falcons flying from Nagaland to southern Africa every year
Migration
A family moving to a new city once
Not migration
items.a: see items
items.why: A migration is a long journey made at the same time every year, and back again. A daily trip, or a single move, is not migration.

items.p: Many scientists think birds that nest in the far north fly south for the winter mainly because of what?
opts: The food runs out in winter
They get bored of one place
Their feathers stop working in the cold
items.why: In winter the northern ground freezes and the insects and plants the birds eat are gone. A bird with enough food can survive a lot of cold, so food is the main reason.

items.p: Match each traveller to their journey.
pairs: Arctic tern
from the Arctic to Antarctica and back
Humpback whale
between cold seas full of krill and warm seas for calves
Monarch butterfly
from Canada to the mountains of Mexico
Demoiselle crane
from Central Asia over the Himalayas to Rajasthan
Hilsa fish
from the Bay of Bengal up rivers to lay eggs
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each of these is a real yearly journey. The Arctic tern's is the longest known.

items.p: Most young birds learn the way on their first journey by following their parents.
items.why: False for many birds. Young cuckoos never meet their parents, and young curlew sandpipers fly south weeks after the adults. They still reach the right part of the world. Some birds, like cranes and geese, do travel as families.

items.p: With your eyes shut, you learn to walk from a mark to a bowl in your usual steps. Then someone moves your start 2 steps to the left, without telling you. Where will you stop, and why?
items.a: About 2 steps to the left of the bowl. My steps go the same way and the same distance as always, so they end in a new place.
items.why: A strong answer says the steps carry a direction and a distance, not the place of the bowl.

items.p: Revathi, a girl in Kochi, does the bowl test. From the secret start, she stops 4 foot-lengths from the bowl. Then she peeks at the bowl for three seconds, and stops 1 foot-length away. What helped her?
opts: She walked faster
She took bigger steps
She knew where the bowl was
items.why: The peek showed her where the bowl was, so she could walk to the place, not just do her steps. This is how older birds who know a place can correct a wrong start.

items.p: Draw the floor from above in your bowl test. Show the bowl, the usual start and the secret start. Draw a dot where you stopped from each start.
items.art: An empty box with a small bowl drawn at the top.
items.a: A drawing with the bowl at one end, two starts side by side, and dots: one near the bowl from the usual start, one off to the side from the secret start.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the second dot shifted sideways by about the same amount as the start.

items.p: A wind that blows from behind you, the way you are going, is called a ____.
items.why: A tailwind pushes a traveller along. A wind in your face is a headwind.

items.p: In the paper butterfly test, the butterfly landed much further with the fan behind her. What does that tell us about real migrating insects?
opts: A tailwind can carry them much further for the same effort
Wind makes insects lighter
Insects can only fly when it is windy
items.why: Moving air carries small flyers along for free. Many insects and birds wait for a tailwind, so the same effort takes them much further.

items.p: Here is a map of a curlew sandpiper's year. Label the two places: 'breeding ground' and 'wintering ground'.
items.art: A simple map with a dot in the far north of Russia and a dot at the tip of Tamil Nadu, joined by a dotted line.
a: The Arctic tundra of Russia: breeding ground
Kodiakkarai in Tamil Nadu: wintering ground
items.why: The breeding ground is where she lays eggs and raises chicks. The wintering ground is where she spends the cold months of the north.

items.p: Put a humpback whale mother's year in order.
items: Her calf is born in the warm sea. She eats almost nothing.
She swims back with her calf to the cold sea to eat.
She eats krill all summer in a cold sea and stores fat.
She swims thousands of kilometres to a warm sea.
a: She eats krill all summer in a cold sea and stores fat.
She swims thousands of kilometres to a warm sea.
Her calf is born in the warm sea. She eats almost nothing.
She swims back with her calf to the cold sea to eat.
items.why: Humpbacks feed in cold seas and raise calves in warm seas. The mother lives on her stored fat while she is in the warm sea.

items.p: Lakshmi, a girl in Madurai, says, 'Migration is easy for birds. They just fly.' Give two reasons why she is not right.
items.a: Migration takes a huge amount of energy, so birds must store fat first. On the way there are storms, hunters, bright lights and dried-up lakes, and many birds die.
items.why: A strong answer gives two different costs: energy, and dangers on the way.

items.p: A lake near Hyderabad has birds from the north every winter. The city wants to build houses on half of the lake.

views.says: Thousands of birds from Russia and Central Asia depend on this lake. If it shrinks, many may not survive the winter.

views.who: Farhan, who needs a house for his family
views.says: The city is growing and people need homes. The birds can go to another lake.
We can build on the land near the road and keep the shallow water, where the birds feed, untouched.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one thing someone from another side would say back.
items.a: Any side, argued with a reason from the unit, then a fair answer from another side.
items.why: A strong answer uses a fact from the unit: birds need stopovers and wintering grounds, and losing one can harm birds from far away. It also takes the families who need homes seriously.

items.p: Three of these help migrating birds. Which one is the odd one out?
opts: Keeping a lake as a resting place
Counting birds and sharing the lists
Leaving bright lights on all night in tall buildings
Stopping hunting on the route
items.why: Bright lights at night confuse birds that fly by the stars, and many crash into lit buildings. The others give birds food, rest or safe passage.

items.p: A young cuckoo is raised by other birds and never meets her parents. In autumn she flies alone to Africa, the right way. What does this tell scientists?
opts: She learned the way from the birds who raised her
The direction was inborn: she had it from birth
She followed other cuckoos she met by chance
items.why: She had nobody to follow or copy, so her direction must have been with her from birth. Scientists call this inborn or innate.

items.p: In the 1950s, A.C. Perdeck moved thousands of starlings from the Netherlands to Switzerland in autumn. The young ones ended up in Spain. The adults reached their usual winter home in the north of France and England. Explain the difference.
items.a: The young birds kept their inborn direction from the new start, so they ended up in the wrong place, like my steps from the secret start. The adults knew where their winter home was, so they turned towards the place.
items.why: A strong answer links the young birds to direction and distance, the adults to knowing the place, and connects it to the bowl test.

items.p: An autumn monarch butterfly lives about as long as a summer one.
items.why: False. Summer monarchs live a few weeks. Autumn monarchs live about 8 months, long enough to fly to Mexico, rest there all winter and start the trip north.

items.p: Why does the monarch journey north take three or four generations?
opts: Each spring and summer monarch lives only a few weeks, so her children carry the journey on
The butterflies get lost and have to start again
The butterflies stop to hide from the rain for months
items.why: Each spring and summer monarch lives only a few weeks. She flies part of the way, lays eggs, and dies. Her children carry the journey further.

items.p: An Arctic tern flies about 70,000 km in a year. She lives 30 years. Roughly how far does she fly in her life, in lakh kilometres?
items.why: 70,000 times 30 is 21,00,000 kilometres, which is 21 lakh. That is like flying to the Moon and back nearly three times.

items.p: Sort these into clues a bird can use to find the way, and things that make finding the way harder.
items: the Sun
Helps find the way
thick cloud
Makes it harder
the stars
Helps find the way
bright city lights
Makes it harder
the Earth's magnetism
Helps find the way
a storm
Makes it harder
a coastline
Helps find the way
items.a: see items
items.why: The Sun, stars, the Earth's magnetism and landmarks guide birds. Clouds hide the Sun and stars, bright lights hide the stars, and storms blow birds off course.

items.p: A paper butterfly is dropped twice from the same height: once in still air, and once with a fan blowing from behind. Why does she land further away with the fan, even though the fall takes about the same time?
items.a: All the time she was falling, the moving air pushed her forward. The fall took about the same time, but now she was moving forward the whole way down, so she landed further away.
items.why: A strong answer separates falling (down) from being pushed (forward), and says the push lasted the whole fall.

items.p: Most humpback whales migrate. Humpbacks in the Arabian Sea stay all year. What is the best explanation?
opts: They have forgotten how to migrate
Their sea gives them enough food and warmth all year
They are a different kind of animal, not a whale
items.why: Animals migrate to find what they need. If the Arabian Sea gives these whales food and warm water all year, there is no need to go. Scientists still study them.

items.p: Label each part of the bowl test with what it stands for in a bird's journey.
items.art: A floor plan with a bowl, two start marks and a dotted line, with five empty label boxes.
a: Usual start: where the bird usually begins
Secret start: where a storm blew her
Counted steps: her inborn direction and distance
The three-second peek: knowing the place
items.why: Each part of the test stands for something real in a young or older bird's journey.

items.p: Scientists want to fix trackers on demoiselle cranes in Rajasthan, to learn their route.

views.says: If we know the route and the stopovers, we can protect them. A light tracker hardly slows a crane down.

views.who: Ravi, a farmer who feeds the cranes
views.says: The cranes come here every year and trust us. Catching them to fix trackers will frighten them.
Trackers are fine if they are very light and fall off later. Then we learn and the cranes are not harmed for long.

items.p: Something you can see, hear or smell that tells you where you are, like a coast or a temple tower, is called a ____.
items.why: Landmarks help older travellers who know a place. Young birds on their first journey have not learned them yet.

items.p: Three of these are on the Central Asian Flyway, a route birds take to India. Which one is the odd one out?
opts: Russia
Kazakhstan
Kodiakkarai in Tamil Nadu
The mountains of Mexico

items.art: Two empty boxes side by side labelled Before and After.
items.a: Two birds: a thin one, and a rounder one with fat under the skin of the belly and chest.
items.why: Birds store fat under the skin as fuel. A strong drawing shows the difference and labels the fat.

items.p: Match each tool to how scientists use it to follow a journey.
pairs: A numbered ring
tells where a bird was before, if she is caught again
A paper tag on a wing
lets anyone who finds the butterfly post the tag back
A satellite tracker
sends the animal's position from anywhere
Weather radar
shows huge flocks flying at night
A bird count by volunteers
shows when travellers arrive and leave
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each tool tells scientists something different. Rings need the bird to be found again. Trackers send their own signals.

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Mysuru, says, 'Birds fly south because they feel cold.' Bidisha, a girl in Kolkata, says, 'They fly south because the food runs out.' Who has the better reason? Use evidence.
items.a: Bidisha has the better reason. Birds with enough food can survive cold, and some kinds stay north where there is food in winter. Migrants go where there is food, and come back when there is plenty again.
items.why: A strong answer chooses food and gives a piece of evidence, such as birds staying where food lasts all winter.

items.p: A young curlew sandpiper is blown 500 km east by a storm over Russia, on her first journey south. Predict where she might end up, and explain why. Then say what an adult would probably do.
items.a: She would keep flying her inborn direction from the new start, so she would land about 500 km east of where her kind usually winters, in the wrong place. An adult who knows the wintering place could correct and turn towards it.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea of direction from a moved start, as in the bowl test and the starling experiment, and contrasts it with knowing a place.

items.p: Globe skimmer dragonflies appear in the Maldives every October. Did they fly there from India?

views.who: Charles Anderson, a marine biologist in the Maldives
views.says: The Maldives have almost no fresh water for dragonflies to breed in. Yet millions arrive each year with the winds from India. They must be crossing the sea.
Nobody has followed a dragonfly across the ocean. We need trackers before we can be sure.
Studies of their wings point to a long journey too. It is very likely, though not proved.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give your reason. Then say what evidence would change your mind.
items.a: Any side, argued with evidence, then a fair answer from another side.
items.why: A strong answer uses the evidence: the arrival with winds from India, the lack of fresh water to breed in, and the wing studies. It also says honestly that no one has followed a single dragonfly the whole way.

items.p: In the bowl test, Arun, a boy in the story, is moved 1 metre to the left and walks his steps. He stops 1 metre to the left of the bowl. His sister moves him 2 metres to the left. Where will he probably stop?
opts: Right at the bowl
About 2 metres to the left of the bowl
About 1 metre to the left of the bowl
items.why: His steps carry the same direction and distance from any start. So the stopping spot moves by the same amount as the start: about 2 metres to the left.

items.p: An autumn monarch flies to forests in Mexico that she has never seen. Her great-great-grandmother left those forests. Some people say, 'The journey is remembered.' Who or what remembers it? Explain your answer.
items.a: The journey is carried in the butterflies' bodies, passed on from parents to children, together with their use of the Sun and their body clock. No single butterfly has done the whole trip, so the knowing must be passed down.
items.why: A strong answer says the direction is inborn and passed down through generations, and admits that exactly how they find the same forests is not fully known.

items.p: In the paper butterfly test, Ananya's butterfly landed 20 cm from the coin with no wind, and 160 cm with the fan behind. How many times further did the tailwind carry her?
items.why: 160 divided by 20 is 8. So the tailwind carried her 8 times as far from the same height.

items.p: A tracker should weigh no more than about 3 parts in every 100 of an animal's weight. A bird weighs 100 grams. What is the heaviest tracker she should carry?
opts: About 3 grams
About 30 grams
About 100 grams
items.why: 3 parts in every 100 of 100 grams is 3 grams. A heavier tracker could tire her or slow her down.

items.p: Scientists know exactly how birds sense the Earth's magnetism.
items.why: False. Many think a protein called cryptochrome in birds' eyes is involved. Others think nerves in the beak or ears help. It is still argued about.

items.p: Your steps worked from the usual start, and a peek worked from anywhere. Which kind of knowing does a young bird use, and which does an older bird have? Why might birds need both?
items.a: A young bird uses a direction and distance, like the counted steps. An older bird also knows places, like the peek. The direction gets a young bird to the right part of the world. Knowing the place lets her correct mistakes and find the exact spot.
items.why: A strong answer names both kinds of knowing, links each to a step in the test, and says what each one is good for.

items.why: The tern, godwit, falcon and monarch journeys have been followed with trackers, rings or tags. The globe skimmer's full route across the ocean has not yet been followed.

items.p: Design a city building that is safer for birds that fly at night. Draw it and label two features.
items.art: An empty box with a city skyline drawn faintly at the bottom.
items.a: A building with lights that are off or shaded at night, glass with patterns birds can see, or no lights pointing up at the sky.
items.why: A strong design deals with the two real dangers: bright lights that confuse night flyers, and glass that birds cannot see.

items.p: Scientists want to find where butterflies go in winter. Put these steps in the order that makes sense.
items: People search there and find forests full of butterflies.
Volunteers stick paper tags on butterflies.
Tagged butterflies are found in those forests.
Tags are posted back from further and further south.
a: Volunteers stick paper tags on butterflies.
Tags are posted back from further and further south.
People search there and find forests full of butterflies.
Tagged butterflies are found in those forests.
items.why: The tags come first, pointing the way. Then people search where the tags point. Finding tagged butterflies in the forests proves the journey.

items.p: Rukmini, a girl in Bengaluru, says, 'If a young bird's direction is inborn, then a bird born to parents who fly south-west will also fly south-west.' What would test her idea?
opts: Ask the parents which way they fly
Count how many eggs the parents lay
Raise young birds away from their parents, and see which way they try to fly at migration time
items.why: To test whether direction is passed from parents, you raise young birds away from their parents and see which way they try to go at migration time. Scientists have done this with small birds called blackcaps.

items.p: A place on the route where a traveller rests and eats before going on is called a ____.
items.why: Stopovers are like petrol stations for travellers. Losing one can harm birds from far away.

items.p: Match each traveller to the danger they face most on their journey.
pairs: Small songbird flying at night
bright city lights and lit glass buildings
Red crab on Christmas Island
cars on the roads to the sea
Bar-headed goose over the Himalayas
very thin, cold air
Young sandpiper on her first journey
storms that blow her off course
Monarch butterfly
fields sprayed with poison, with no milkweed
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each journey has its own dangers. Knowing them helps people protect the travellers.

items.p: Humans are animals too. Give an example of a group of people in India who migrate every year, and say how their reason is like a bird's reason.
items.a: Gaddi shepherds in Himachal Pradesh take their flocks up to the high meadows in summer and down in winter. Like birds, they go where there is food for their animals at each time of year.
items.why: A strong answer names a real group and links the reason to food, water or a safe place, as for other animals.

applications: Bird scientists and forest staff protect wetlands like Chilika Lake, Pulicat Lake and Point Calimere, because birds from far away depend on them.
Countries along a flyway agree to protect the travellers together, because one bird needs safe places in many countries.
Some cities dim building lights in the migration months so night-flying birds are not confused.
Weather radar is used to see big nights of bird migration, and to keep birds and aeroplanes apart near airports.
Villagers in Khichan, Rajasthan, feed thousands of demoiselle cranes every winter, and visitors come to see them.
In Bangladesh, fishing is banned for some days each year while hilsa swim up the rivers to lay their eggs.
Volunteers count birds in Indian cities and villages and share the lists online, helping scientists see when travellers arrive.
Engineers design road tunnels and bridges for travelling animals, like the crab bridges on Christmas Island.

open_questions.q: How is a young bird's direction and distance passed down from her parents?

open_questions.q: How do monarch great-great-grandchildren find the very same mountain forests?

open_questions.why_open: Many are too small to carry trackers, so their routes are still being worked out from rings and bird counts.

maths.problem: In the bowl test, Harini's three walks from the usual start ended 1, 2 and 1 foot-lengths from the bowl. Her three walks from the secret start ended 4, 5 and 4 foot-lengths away. On average, how many more foot-lengths away was she from the secret start?
maths.explain: From the usual start: 1 + 2 + 1 = 4, shared over 3 walks is a little more than 1 each. From the secret start: 4 + 5 + 4 = 13, a little more than 4 each. 4 take away 1 is 3. So she stopped about 3 foot-lengths further away, about as far as she had been moved.
maths.why_maths: Comparing totals over three tries shows the real difference, not a fluke from one try.
maths.context: This is about the bowl test, where you walked counted steps from the usual start and from a secret start.

maths.problem: In the paper butterfly test, the butterfly landed 15 cm, 25 cm and 20 cm from the coin with no wind. With the fan behind, she landed 120 cm, 160 cm and 140 cm away. Is the tailwind effect real, or could it be a fluke?
maths.answer: Real. Every wind drop was further than every no-wind drop.
maths.explain: The longest no-wind drop was 25 cm. The shortest wind drop was 120 cm. Even the worst wind drop was nearly 5 times the best no-wind drop. If the wind made no difference, the two sets would overlap.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the biggest of one set with the smallest of the other tells us whether a difference is real.
maths.context: This is about the paper butterfly test, where you dropped a paper butterfly with and without a fan behind her.

chart.title: Paper butterfly: average distance from the coin

maths.problem: A humpback whale swims about 8,000 km from a cold sea to a warm sea, and the same distance back. How far is that in one year?
maths.explain: 8,000 km there and 8,000 km back. 8,000 + 8,000 = 16,000 km. India is about 3,200 km from Kashmir to Kanyakumari, so that is about five times the length of India.
maths.why_maths: Adding the two halves of a journey shows how far a migrant really goes in a year.
maths.context: This is about humpback whales, who swim between cold seas and warm seas each year.

maths.problem: Monarch butterflies leave Mexico in March. The journey north takes about 4 generations, and each generation lives about 1 month. In about which month do they reach Canada?
maths.explain: Start in March and count 4 months on: April, May, June, July. So they reach Canada in about July. The exact timing changes from year to year.
maths.why_maths: Counting months on a calendar shows how a journey can take longer than one butterfly's life.
maths.context: This is about the monarch butterfly's journey north, which takes several generations.

maths.problem: Scientists use a rule that a tracker can weigh no more than 3 grams for every 100 grams of bird. A pigeon weighs about 300 grams. What is the heaviest tracker she should carry?
maths.explain: 300 grams is 3 groups of 100 grams. Each group allows 3 grams. 3 groups of 3 grams is 9 grams. A small sandpiper of about 60 grams could carry less than 2 grams.
maths.why_maths: Counting equal groups tells scientists how heavy a tracker can safely be for each bird.
maths.context: This is about trackers, the tiny machines that scientists fix on birds to follow their journeys.

roots.context: We have met animals who cross half the world every year. A young bird on her first journey reaches the right part of the world without being shown the way. Your bowl test showed that there are two different ways to find your way.

deep_truth.truth: From the secret start, your usual steps stopped about as far from the bowl as you were moved. Your steps held a direction and a distance, and nothing about where the bowl was. A young bird on her first journey flies a direction and distance she was born with. So a storm that moves her can send her to the wrong country.
deep_truth.habit: We talk about 'knowing the way' as one thing, as if it were a map in the head. Your test split it into two: a direction and distance, which works only from the usual start, and knowing the place, which works from anywhere.
deep_truth.evidence: From the usual start, your steps stopped near the bowl. From the secret start, they stopped about as far from the bowl as you had been moved. A three-second peek brought you back. Perdeck's young starlings, moved from the Netherlands to Switzerland, kept their direction and ended up in Spain, while the adults turned towards their usual winter home.

three.who_am_i: You find your way in both ways every day: by counting steps or turns, and by knowing places, their sights, sounds and smells. You are a navigating animal, like the tern and the whale.
three.what_is_life: Some journeys are longer than one life. The monarchs who fly north in spring are not the ones who reach Canada. Their great-grandchildren are. The journey is carried on from parents to children, inside their bodies.
three.what_is_this_world: A mudflat in Tamil Nadu and the Arctic tundra in Russia are joined every year by the same small birds. To a sandpiper, they are two ends of one home.

roots.thread: A young bird carries a direction inside her from birth. An older bird also knows the places she has been. Your steps and your peek were these two kinds of knowing. One is carried by the traveller wherever she goes. The other belongs to a place, and is learned by being there.

teachings.teaching: The stork in the sky knows her appointed times. The turtledove, the swift and the crane keep the time of their coming.
teachings.link: About 2,600 years ago, people already saw that storks, doves, swifts and cranes leave and return at the same time every year, without being taught. Today we know that young birds are born with a timing and a direction.

teachings.source: Kalidasa, Meghaduta (The Cloud Messenger), first part, verse 11 (numbering differs a little between editions)
teachings.teaching: When they hear the cloud's thunder, the royal swans, longing for Lake Manasa, fly with the cloud through the sky as far as Mount Kailasa, carrying pieces of lotus stalk as food for the journey.
teachings.link: Bar-headed geese leave India in spring for lakes on the Tibetan plateau, the same high country as Mount Kailasa. A long journey really does need food stored for the way: real birds carry it as fat.

teachings.teaching: When the great bird Peng flies to the southern sea, Peng beats the water for three thousand li and rises on the whirlwind, and sets off on the winds of the sixth month.
teachings.link: Peng waits for the right wind before leaving. Real migrants do the same: radar shows many more birds take off when the wind blows their way. Your paper butterfly showed why.

science.text: Many young birds on their first migration fly an inborn direction, for an inborn length of time, without being shown the way.
Older birds also learn places and can correct for being moved. Young birds usually cannot.
Birds use the Sun, the stars, the Earth's magnetism and landmarks to find their way.
How birds sense the Earth's magnetism, and how an inborn direction is carried in the body, are still being worked out.
Whether globe skimmer dragonflies cross the ocean from India to Africa and back is very likely, but not yet proved.

other_view.view: A young bird's inborn direction is a program carried in her genes, shaped over millions of years by which birds survived the journey. They call it an instinct, and would rather not use the word 'knowing' for it.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, nobody knew where the monarch butterflies of North America went in winter. Every autumn, millions of them flew south from Canada and the United States, and then they seemed to vanish. Many people did not believe that a butterfly, as light as a flower petal, could fly thousands of kilometres. In the 1950s, Norah Urquhart and Fred Urquhart, two scientists in Canada, asked ordinary people for help. Thousands of volunteers stuck tiny paper tags on the wings of monarchs. Each tag had a number and an address. When someone found a tagged butterfly, they posted the tag back and said where they found it. Year by year, the tags pointed further south, towards Mexico. In January 1975, Catalina Aguado, a young woman from Mexico, and Ken Brugger, an American who was helping the Urquharts, climbed into the mountains of central Mexico. There they found fir trees covered in millions of resting monarchs. The local people had known about them for generations. Later, butterflies carrying tags from the United States were found in those forests. A butterfly really could fly that far.
how_we_found_out.who: Norah and Fred Urquhart, Canadian scientists; Catalina Aguado and Ken Brugger, who found the winter forests; thousands of volunteer taggers; and the local people of the Mexican mountains, who knew about the butterflies all along
how_we_found_out.when: 1950s (the tagging began) and January 1975 (the winter forests were found)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many people did not believe that a butterfly could fly thousands of kilometres. Tags posted back from further and further south, and then tagged butterflies found in the Mexican forests, showed that monarchs really do.
